title: Why Culture Matters in the EFL Classroom
brief: Open the unit by establishing why cultural awareness is a practical classroom management concern, not merely an abstract ideal. Draw on the module's framing of the 'observe, evaluate, adapt, act' cycle and its emphasis on helping teachers 'adapt materials and techniques to suit their own teaching needs' and 'apply those observations to their own teaching contexts.' Use the module's description of classrooms from 'around the world' spanning very young learners through adults to illustrate that no single classroom norm is universal. The section should set a humble, grounded tone: the teacher is a learner of context, not an authority on another culture.

title: Classroom Expectations and Physical Space Across Contexts
brief: Focus on how the physical arrangement of a classroom both reflects and shapes cultural expectations about learning. Draw directly on the module's warm-up activity asking teachers to draw an 'ideal classroom,' consider 'all the parts (ceilings, floors, walls, etc.)' and the 'arrangement of other resources,' and then discuss 'why would teachers arrange their rooms like your picture?' and 'how do the features you included help students learn and facilitate classroom management?' Use the module's contrast between the 'large and well-equipped' US bilingual classroom and the prompt asking teachers what to do 'if your classroom environment is not like the one in the video.' The section should help the reader see that what feels 'normal' in a classroom layout is culturally shaped, and that adapting to a new context starts with observation rather than assumption.

title: Participation Norms and Learner Autonomy
brief: Examine how expectations about student participation — who speaks, when, and how — vary across teaching contexts, and how a teacher can adapt without imposing a single model. Ground this in the module's definition of learner autonomy as 'the ability of students to make decisions about and direct their own learning,' and the module's discussion of how 'establishing routines can help younger students become more well-behaved and autonomous learners.' Draw on the module's questions about how teachers can 'call on students to share information' and 'get more than one student to answer each question,' as well as the discussion of learning stations as a structure that offers student choice. The section should acknowledge that high levels of student-directed activity may feel unfamiliar in some cultural contexts and encourage the teacher to introduce such approaches gradually and reflectively.

title: Attitudes to Authority, Feedback, and Error
brief: Address how cultural context shapes learner attitudes toward the teacher's authority and toward making mistakes in public. Use the module's definition of feedback as 'the information that lets learners know how they are doing,' noting that 'either the teacher or other learners can provide feedback in oral or written form.' Draw on the module's treatment of encouragement as 'pointing out areas for improvement in a supportive way' and the Costa Rica classroom example where 'the teacher gives positive feedback to students when they answer questions correctly' and 'manages situations involving distractions and off-task students.' The section should help the reader think about how the same feedback technique can land very differently depending on learners' prior experience of authority, and encourage the teacher to observe before deciding how directive or collaborative to be.

title: Adapting Without Stereotyping: The Reflective Teacher
brief: Bring together the unit's practical thread by focusing on the habit of reflective adaptation as the antidote to both cultural ignorance and cultural stereotyping. Draw on the module's 'observe, evaluate, adapt, act' cycle and its explicit goal of helping teachers 'reflect on what they have learned' and 'act upon insights gained.' Use the module's recommendation to 'keep notes or an informal reflective log of what you feel went well with the training and what you would like to do differently next time' as a concrete tool. Emphasise the module's framing that the guides 'can be completed in any order' and are designed for 'both new and experienced EFL teachers,' reinforcing that cultural adaptation is an ongoing process rather than a one-time orientation. The section should close with a practical prompt for the reader to begin their own reflective log focused on one cultural difference they have already noticed in their classroom.
